p: We have tablets in our class. We use them to read and play maths games. When we finish, we put them back on the charger.
Being safe online is important. Never tell strangers your name or where you live. If something makes you feel worried, tell a grown up.
Our class made a robot move. We told it to go forward, turn and stop. It drove all the way to the door.
I like to take photos with my mum's camera. I took pictures of flowers and birds. We printed my best photo.
Too much screen time is not good for us. After school I play outside first. Then I can have some time on the tablet.
My grandpa lives far away. We call him on video every Sunday. He shows me his garden and his chickens.

p: Your digital footprint is all the information about you that exists online. It includes photos, comments, game usernames and the websites you visit. Once something is posted, it can be hard to remove. That is why it is smart to think carefully before you share anything online.

Our class learned to code using blocks on the computer. We made a game where a character collects stars and avoids monsters. When our code did not work, we looked for the bug and fixed it. Debugging taught us to be patient and to try again.

Cyberbullying is when someone uses technology to hurt, embarrass or threaten another person. It can happen through messages, games or social media. If you are cyberbullied, do not reply. Take a screenshot, block the person and tell a trusted adult straight away.

A strong password helps keep your accounts safe. Instead of using your name or birthday, try using a long phrase made of random words, numbers and symbols. Never share your password with friends, and use a different password for each important account.

Robots are used in many places today. In factories they build cars, in hospitals they help surgeons, and on Mars they explore the surface. Some robots can even vacuum floors at home. Engineers keep finding new ways for robots to help people.

Not everything on the internet is true. Some websites share false information on purpose, and some photos are edited. To check if something is reliable, look at who made the website, compare it with other sources and ask a teacher or parent if you are unsure.

s: Artificial intelligence learns patterns from large amounts of data, which means biased data can lead to biased results.
Two-factor authentication adds an extra layer of protection to your online accounts.

Phishing scams use fake emails and websites to trick people into revealing personal information.
The eSafety Commissioner helps Australians deal with online abuse and harmful content.

Deepfakes are videos created with artificial intelligence that can make people appear to say things they never said.
Data privacy laws control how companies collect, store and use personal information.

Many apps are designed to keep users scrolling for as long as possible.
Engineers use the design process: define the problem, brainstorm, build a prototype, test and improve.
Cloud storage allows files to be saved on remote servers and accessed from anywhere.
Online gaming can build teamwork and problem-solving skills when played in moderation.

Software updates often fix security weaknesses that hackers could exploit.

Screen time before bed can delay sleep because blue light affects the body clock.
Technology itself is neither good nor bad; it depends on how people choose to use it.
p: Social media platforms use algorithms to decide what each user sees. These algorithms track what you like, comment on and watch, then show you more of the same. While this can make feeds feel personalised, it can also create filter bubbles where people only see views similar to their own. Being aware of this helps users seek out a range of perspectives.

Phishing is a type of scam in which criminals pretend to be a trusted organisation, such as a bank or delivery company. They send messages that create a sense of urgency, asking people to click a link or enter their password. Warning signs include spelling mistakes, unusual sender addresses and requests for personal information. When in doubt, contact the organisation directly.

Artificial intelligence is already part of daily life, from voice assistants to recommendation systems. AI systems learn by finding patterns in large amounts of data. However, if the data contains biases, the AI can repeat or even amplify them. For example, a hiring tool trained on past decisions might unfairly favour certain groups. Careful design and testing are needed to make AI fair.

The engineering design process helps people solve problems in a structured way. First, engineers define the problem and research what is needed. Next, they brainstorm ideas and choose the most promising one. They build a prototype, test it and gather feedback. Based on the results, they improve the design. This cycle may repeat many times before a final product is ready.

Online safety involves more than avoiding strangers. It includes protecting your personal information, using strong passwords, thinking before you post and knowing how to report harmful content. Australia's eSafety Commissioner provides resources and can help remove cyberbullying material. Talking openly with family about online experiences makes it easier to ask for help when something goes wrong.

Electronic waste, such as old phones, computers and televisions, contains valuable materials like gold, copper and rare earth metals, as well as toxic substances like lead. When e-waste is thrown into landfill, these materials are wasted and chemicals can leak into the soil. Recycling programs recover useful materials safely, and repairing devices extends their life and reduces waste.

s: Generative artificial intelligence raises complex questions about authorship, copyright and the value of human creativity.
The attention economy rewards platforms for capturing as much user time as possible, sometimes at the expense of wellbeing.
Algorithmic decision-making in areas such as policing and lending must be transparent and accountable.
Cybersecurity has become a matter of national security as critical infrastructure grows increasingly connected.
Data has been described as the new oil, though critics argue the comparison obscures questions of consent.
Misinformation spreads faster than corrections because false stories are often more novel and emotionally charged.
The digital divide means that unequal access to technology can deepen existing educational and economic inequalities.
Australia's social media age restrictions have sparked debate about enforcement, privacy and young people's rights.
Quantum computers may eventually break current encryption methods, prompting research into new security standards.
Ethical design considers the consequences of technology for users, communities and the environment.
Surveillance capitalism describes business models that profit from collecting and analysing personal behaviour.
Open-source software allows anyone to inspect, modify and distribute code, encouraging collaboration and innovation.
Automation may increase productivity, yet its benefits will not automatically be shared fairly across society.
Regulating global technology companies is challenging because their operations cross national borders.
Media literacy equips citizens to evaluate sources, recognise manipulation and resist propaganda.
The environmental cost of data centres, including energy and water use, is growing rapidly.
Facial recognition technology offers security benefits but poses serious risks to privacy and civil liberties.
Human oversight remains essential when artificial intelligence is used in high-stakes decisions.
Ransomware attacks have targeted hospitals, universities and businesses, demanding payment to restore data.
Digital identity systems promise convenience but must be designed to protect against misuse and data breaches.
Technological change often outpaces the ability of laws and institutions to adapt.
Persuasive design techniques, such as infinite scroll, can make it difficult for users to disconnect.

Innovation flourishes when diverse teams bring different perspectives to complex problems.
Responsible technology requires asking not only whether something can be built, but whether it should be.
p: Generative artificial intelligence can now produce essays, images, music and computer code in seconds. Supporters believe these tools will boost productivity and make creative expression more accessible. Critics raise concerns about the use of copyrighted material in training data, the potential for large-scale misinformation and the impact on creative professions. Schools and workplaces are grappling with how to integrate these tools responsibly while preserving skills such as independent thinking and original writing.

Misinformation, false information spread without intent to deceive, and disinformation, false information spread deliberately, pose significant challenges for democratic societies. Research suggests that false stories often travel faster online because they are surprising or provoke strong emotions. Responses include fact-checking, platform policies that limit the spread of harmful content and education in media literacy. However, efforts to restrict false information must be balanced against the protection of free expression.

Cybersecurity is no longer just a technical issue for IT departments. Attacks on hospitals, energy networks and government agencies can disrupt essential services and endanger lives. Several major data breaches in Australia have exposed the personal information of millions of people, prompting stronger privacy penalties. Experts emphasise that security depends on both technology and human behaviour, as many breaches begin with a single person clicking a malicious link.

The digital divide refers to the gap between those who have reliable access to technology and the internet and those who do not. In Australia, people in remote communities, older Australians and low-income households are more likely to be digitally excluded. As essential services, education and employment move online, this divide can reinforce disadvantage. Closing it requires investment in infrastructure, affordable access and digital skills training.

Persuasive technology uses insights from psychology to influence behaviour. Features such as notifications, streaks, autoplay and infinite scroll are designed to maximise engagement, which in turn drives advertising revenue. While these designs are not inherently harmful, they can make it difficult for users, particularly young people, to regulate their own use. Some designers advocate for humane technology that respects users' time, attention and wellbeing.

Governing artificial intelligence presents a novel regulatory challenge. Systems may behave unpredictably, their decision-making can be difficult to explain and their effects may cross national borders. Some jurisdictions have adopted risk-based approaches, placing stricter requirements on applications used in areas such as employment, healthcare and law enforcement. Effective governance will likely require collaboration between governments, industry, researchers and civil society to ensure that technological progress serves the public good.
